justification_text:
The point estimates for each forecast horizon (1-day, 1-week, and 1-month) were primarily based on historical data trends, assuming relatively stable conditions and no major disruptions. The assumption is that the variable being forecasted (perhaps a stock price or another metric) will exhibit a central tendency to revert toward levels indicative of its past movement. In this case, the point estimate remains constant at 195.72 across all horizons. This implies that, on average, the expected value of the variable did not shift significantly over time, even when projecting further out. It reflects the belief that, while short-term deviations or fluctuations might occur, the mean expectation stays anchored barring major shocks.

The size of the confidence intervals at each horizon stems mainly from increasing uncertainty over time. For the 1-day forecast, uncertainty is relatively low because there is limited time for substantial changes, so the confidence interval (190.85 to 200.59) is narrow. However, for the 1-week and 1-month forecasts, more factors can influence outcomes, such as market volatility, unforeseen events, or larger systemic shifts. Accordingly, the confidence intervals widen progressively, with the 1-month forecast reflecting the most uncertainty (175.15 to 216.29). In essence, as the prediction horizon grows longer, our ability to confidently estimate future values diminishes due to the accumulation of potential unknowns.

Certain risks or events could push the actual outcomes outside these stated intervals. These include unexpected events such as geopolitical crises, sudden regulatory changes, natural disasters, or company-specific events if this forecast relates to a stock or financial instrument. Large-scale market shocks, like an economic recession announcement or significant interest rate changes by a central bank, could also exert influence. These types of rare but impactful "tail risks" are hard to predict and could lead to outcomes significantly beyond what is captured in the 90% confidence intervals. Thus, while the confidence intervals account for a range of normal fluctuations, extreme scenarios always remain a possibility.
